claim: Trophic eggs play a role in caste determination in the harvester ant Pogonomyrmex rugosus.
source: Here, we show that trophic eggs, which do not contain an embryo and are primarily regarded as a source of food, play a role in the process of caste determination in the harvester ant Pogonomyrmex rugosus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential caste development based on trophic egg presence.

claim: First instar larvae given access to trophic eggs mostly developed into workers.
source: When first instar larvae were given access to trophic eggs, they mostly developed into workers.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the larval caste fate experiment.

claim: Larvae without access to trophic eggs developed into queens.
source: By contrast, larvae without access to trophic eggs developed into queens.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the larval caste fate experiment.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in texture from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by observational and experimental data on egg characteristics.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in morphology from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by observational and experimental data on egg characteristics.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in protein content from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of protein concentrations.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in triglyceride content from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of triglyceride concentrations.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in glycogen content from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of glycogen concentrations.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in sugar content from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of glucose concentrations.

claim: Trophic eggs differ in small RNA content from viable eggs.
source: We found that trophic eggs differ in many ways from viable eggs, including texture, morphology, and their contents of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, sugar, and small RNAs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of small RNA concentrations.

claim: There are differences in the composition of miRNAs between trophic and viable eggs.
source: Moreover, comparison of miRNA fragment size distributions suggests differences in the composition of miRNAs between the two egg types.
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis and Mantel test showing significant differences in miRNA fragment size distribution.

claim: This is the first demonstration of trophic eggs playing a role in caste determination in social insects.
source: This is the first demonstration of trophic eggs playing a role in caste determination in social insects.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their experimental findings.

claim: Trophic eggs do not contain an embryo.
source: Many species of insects, spiders, amphibians, marine invertebrates, and sharks produce trophic eggs, a special type of eggs that do not contain an embryo (Levin and Bridges, 1995; Blake and Arnofsky, 1999; Collin, 2004; Kudo and Nakahira, 2004; Perry and Roitberg, 2006; Strathmann and Strathmann, 2006; Gibson et al., 2012; López-Ortega and Williams, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by experimental observations in this study.

claim: Non-developing eggs are generally assumed to be either a by-product of failed reproduction or serve as nutrition for offspring.
source: It is generally assumed that these non-developing eggs are either a by-product of failed reproduction or that they serve as nutrition for offspring (Perry and Roitberg, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The suggestion that trophic eggs solely provide a nutritional function is based on surprisingly little evidence.
source: However, the suggestion that trophic eggs solely provide a nutritional function is based on surprisingly little evidence.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Trophic eggs have been reported in many ant species.
source: Trophic eggs have been reported in many ant species (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1, table 1) and are generally thought to mostly or only serve as food for offspring (Crespi, 1977; Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1 and supplementary table.

claim: Trophic eggs are generally thought to mostly or only serve as food for offspring.
source: Trophic eggs have been reported in many ant species (Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1, table 1) and are generally thought to mostly or only serve as food for offspring (Crespi, 1977; Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trophic eggs play an important role during the time of colony founding.
source: Trophic eggs play an important role during the time of colony founding (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In most ant species, queens do not forage after the mating flight.
source: Because in most ant species, queens do not forage after the mating flight, they metabolize the alary muscles and fat bodies and convert them into eggs, which serve as food to rear the first batch of larvae (Huber, 1905; Keller and Passera, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Queens metabolize the alary muscles and fat bodies and convert them into eggs, which serve as food to rear the first batch of larvae.
source: Because in most ant species, queens do not forage after the mating flight, they metabolize the alary muscles and fat bodies and convert them into eggs, which serve as food to rear the first batch of larvae (Huber, 1905; Keller and Passera, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Queens generally stop producing trophic eggs after the eclosion of the first workers, except for a few species such as Crematogaster smithi and Acanthomyrmex ferox.
source: Except for a few species such as Crematogaster smithi (Heinze et al., 1995) and Acanthomyrmex ferox (Gobin and Ito, 2000), the queens generally stop producing trophic eggs after the eclosion of the first workers (see Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1, table 1).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1 and supplementary table.

claim: The absence of trophic eggs has been reported in only one species.
source: So far, the absence of trophic eggs has been reported in only one species (Supplementary file 1, table 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary table.

claim: In many ant species, workers are capable of producing haploid males but lack a spermatheca and the ability to produce diploid female offspring.
source: In many ant species, workers are capable of producing haploid males but lack a spermatheca and the ability to produce diploid female offspring (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990; Bourke, 1988; Hammond and Keller, 2004; Wenseleers and Ratnieks, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In some species, workers lay trophic eggs.
source: In some species, workers further lay trophic eggs (see Supplementary file 1, table 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary table.

claim: In genera such as Pogonomyrmex where there is no or only little trophallaxis among workers, trophic eggs may play an important role in food distribution within the colony.
source: These eggs have a trophic function, in particular in genera such as Pogonomyrmex where there is no or only little trophallaxis (regurgitative food sharing) among workers. In such species, it has been suggested that trophic eggs may play an important role in food distribution within the colony (Gobin and Ito, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In the Argentine ant Linepithema humile, the presence of queens in colonies was associated with a drastic decrease in the number of worker-laid trophic eggs as well as a decrease in the proportion of larvae developing into queens.
source: A study in the Argentine ant Linepithema humile showed that the presence of queens in colonies was associated with a drastic decrease in the number of worker-laid trophic eggs as well as a decrease in the proportion of larvae developing into queens (Bartels, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Bartels proposed that trophic eggs may increase the probability of larvae to develop into queens in Linepithema humile.
source: Bartels thus proposed that trophic eggs may increase the probability of larvae to develop into queens, which are much larger than workers (Bartels, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In some lineages of Pogonomyrmex barbatus, queens laid a higher proportion of trophic eggs upon the experimental increase of maternal juvenile hormone.
source: In some lineages of Pogonomyrmex barbatus, queens laid a higher proportion of trophic eggs upon the experimental increase of maternal juvenile hormone (Helms Cahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In Pogonomyrmex barbatus, juvenile hormone treatment strongly reduced the number of workers produced but triggered a 50% increase in worker body size.
source: Because the treatment also strongly reduced the number of workers produced but triggered a 50% increase in worker body size, trophic eggs were suggested to affect worker size.
evidence: Supported by inference from cited study.

claim: Trophic eggs were suggested to affect worker size in Pogonomyrmex barbatus.
source: Because the treatment also strongly reduced the number of workers produced but triggered a 50% increase in worker body size, trophic eggs were suggested to affect worker size.
evidence: Supported by inference from cited study.

claim: An increase in the proportion of trophic eggs has been suggested to be associated with an increase in the proportion of larvae developing into queens in L. humile and P. barbatus.
source: An increase in the proportion of trophic eggs has also been suggested to be associated with an increase in the proportion of larvae developing into queens (L. humile: Bartels, 1988; P. barbatus: Helms Cahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Pogonomyrmex badius, nitrogen content increases with increasing female caste size.
source: Finally, because they observed an increase in nitrogen content with increasing female caste size in the ant Pogonomyrmex badius, Smith and Suarez, 2010 suggested that the larger castes may consume more trophic (nutritional) eggs than the smaller caste, which would feed more on foraged insects.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Smith and Suarez suggested that larger castes may consume more trophic eggs than the smaller caste in Pogonomyrmex badius.
source: Finally, because they observed an increase in nitrogen content with increasing female caste size in the ant Pogonomyrmex badius, Smith and Suarez, 2010 suggested that the larger castes may consume more trophic (nutritional) eggs than the smaller caste, which would feed more on foraged insects.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In at least three species of ants, trophic eggs may play a role in the developmental trajectories of female larvae.
source: In summary, in at least three species of ants, trophic eggs may play a role in the developmental trajectories of female larvae.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies on L. humile, P. barbatus, and P. badius.

claim: During egg cross-fostering experiments in Pogonomyrmex rugosus, there was a sudden increase in the frequency of females developing into queens when trophic eggs were discarded.
source: While conducting egg cross-fostering experiments in the ant Pogonomyrmex rugosus to study worker size variation, we observed a sudden increase in the frequency of females developing into queens. During these experiments, we discarded trophic eggs and only cross-fostered eggs that would eventually hatch (hereafter viable eggs).
evidence: Supported by observational data from experiments.

claim: The absence of trophic eggs may have influenced the process of caste determination in Pogonomyrmex rugosus.
source: This raises the possibility that the absence of trophic eggs influenced the process of caste determination.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The presence of trophic eggs reduces the probability that female larvae develop into reproductive individuals in P. rugosus.
source: Our experiments revealed that the presence of trophic eggs reduces the probability that female larvae develop into reproductive individuals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the larval caste fate experiment.

claim: Viable eggs in P. rugosus are white with a bright surface and have a distinct oval shape.
source: Viable eggs are white with a bright surface and have a distinct oval shape, a homogenous content as well as a solid chorion (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2A.

claim: Viable eggs have a homogenous content.
source: Viable eggs are white with a bright surface and have a distinct oval shape, a homogenous content as well as a solid chorion (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2A.

claim: Viable eggs have a solid chorion.
source: Viable eggs are white with a bright surface and have a distinct oval shape, a homogenous content as well as a solid chorion (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2A.

claim: Trophic eggs are rounder than viable eggs.
source: while trophic eggs are rounder, have a smooth surface and a granular-looking content as well as a fragile chorion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2D.

claim: Trophic eggs have a smooth surface.
source: while trophic eggs are rounder, have a smooth surface and a granular-looking content as well as a fragile chorion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2D.

claim: Trophic eggs have a granular-looking content.
source: while trophic eggs are rounder, have a smooth surface and a granular-looking content as well as a fragile chorion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2D.

claim: Trophic eggs have a fragile chorion.
source: while trophic eggs are rounder, have a smooth surface and a granular-looking content as well as a fragile chorion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figure 2D.

claim: Trophic eggs had a significantly larger volume (94.3 ± 4.3 nL) than viable eggs (63.3 ± 1.6 nl).
source: Trophic eggs had a significantly larger volume (94.3 ± 4.3 nL; n = 11) than viable eggs (n = 14; 63.3 ± 1.6 nl; two-sample t-test, t(23) = –9.54, p = 1.8 × 10–09).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Viable eggs showed embryonic development at 25 and 65 hr.
source: While viable eggs showed embryonic development at 25 and 65 hr (Figure 2B and C) there was no such development for trophic eggs (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Trophic eggs showed no embryonic development at 25 and 65 hr.
source: While viable eggs showed embryonic development at 25 and 65 hr (Figure 2B and C) there was no such development for trophic eggs (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Supported by observational data and Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: P. rugosus workers only laid viable eggs.
source: P. rugosus workers only laid viable eggs.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: P. rugosus workers started to lay eggs approximately 3 weeks after queen removal.
source: They started to lay eggs approximately 3 weeks after queen removal (n = 12 queenless recipient colonies), and approximately 90% of the eggs successfully hatched.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Approximately 90% of worker-laid eggs successfully hatched.
source: They started to lay eggs approximately 3 weeks after queen removal (n = 12 queenless recipient colonies), and approximately 90% of the eggs successfully hatched.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Only approximately 5% of worker-laid eggs successfully developed into pupae which were all males.
source: However, only approximately 5% successfully developed into pupae which were all males.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: The percentage of eggs that were trophic was higher before hibernation (61.6 ± 1.4%) than after (50.3 ± 2.0%).
source: The percentage of eggs that were trophic was higher before hibernation (61.6 ± 1.4% mean ± SE; n = 43 colonies) than after (50.3 ± 2.0%; LMER, t(86) = 5.04, p = 9 × 10–6).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The production of viable and trophic eggs was not random.
source: The production of the two types of eggs was not random (Wald–Wolfowitz runs tests, p-values for the 11 queens in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using Wald-Wolfowitz runs tests.

claim: Each of the 11 queens tended to lay relatively long sequences of either viable (6.1 ± 0.7) or trophic eggs (6.0 ± 0.5).
source: Instead, each of the 11 queens tended to lay relatively long sequences of either viable (6.1 ± 0.7; mean number per sequence ± SE) or trophic eggs (6.0 ± 0.5; Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and Figure 3.

claim: The concentrations of protein were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs.
source: The concentrations of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, and glucose were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs (LMER, protein: t = –13.11, p < 0.0001; triglycerides: t = –11.66, p < 0.0001; glycogen: t = –11.98, p < 0.0001; glucose: t = –18.60, p < 0.0001; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements, statistical analysis, and Figure 4.

claim: The concentrations of triglycerides were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs.
source: The concentrations of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, and glucose were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs (LMER, protein: t = –13.11, p < 0.0001; triglycerides: t = –11.66, p < 0.0001; glycogen: t = –11.98, p < 0.0001; glucose: t = –18.60, p < 0.0001; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements, statistical analysis, and Figure 4.

claim: The concentrations of glycogen were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs.
source: The concentrations of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, and glucose were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs (LMER, protein: t = –13.11, p < 0.0001; triglycerides: t = –11.66, p < 0.0001; glycogen: t = –11.98, p < 0.0001; glucose: t = –18.60, p < 0.0001; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements, statistical analysis, and Figure 4.

claim: The concentrations of glucose were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs.
source: The concentrations of protein, triglycerides, glycogen, and glucose were significantly higher in viable than trophic eggs (LMER, protein: t = –13.11, p < 0.0001; triglycerides: t = –11.66, p < 0.0001; glycogen: t = –11.98, p < 0.0001; glucose: t = –18.60, p < 0.0001; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements, statistical analysis, and Figure 4.

claim: The amount of small RNA was significantly higher in viable eggs (44.3 ± 1.4 ng) than in trophic eggs (22.3 ± 1.1 ng).
source: The amount of small RNA (<200 nt, including miRNA and tRNA; Nagano and Fraser, 2011) was significantly higher in viable eggs (44.3 ± 1.4 ng, mean ± SE) than in trophic eggs (22.3 ± 1.1 ng; paired t-test, t(23) = 15.9, p = 6.5 × 10–14).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The amount of longer RNAs (>200 nt) was significantly higher in viable eggs (7.6 ± 0.6 ng) than in trophic eggs (3.6 ± 0.3 ng).
source: The same was true for longer RNAs (>200 nt; viable eggs: 7.6 ± 0.6 ng, mean ± SE; trophic eggs: 3.6 ± 0.3 ng; paired t-test, t(23) = 7.2, p = 2.7 × 10–7).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The amount of DNA was about twice as high in viable eggs (15.9 ± 1.9 ng/µl) than trophic eggs (8.8 ± 1.9 ng/µl).
source: The DNA quantification showed that the amount of DNA was about twice as high in viable (15.9 ± 1.9 ng/µl) than trophic eggs (8.8 ± 1.9 ng/µl; t-test, t(4.7) = 2.7, p = 0.045).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference in the miRNA fragment size distribution between viable and trophic eggs.
source: There was a significant difference in the miRNA fragment size distribution between viable and trophic eggs (Mantel test, rM = 0.26, p < 0.0001), as shown on the PCA (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 5A.

claim: There was no difference in the tRNA fragment size distribution between viable and trophic eggs.
source: There was no difference in the tRNA fragment size distribution between the two types of eggs (Mantel test, rM = 0.01, p = 0.30, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 5B.

claim: The percentage of larvae that developed into queens was significantly lower in recipient colonies that received trophic eggs (27 ± 9%) than in recipient colonies without trophic eggs (83 ± 10%).
source: The percentage of larvae that developed into queens was significantly lower in recipient colonies that received trophic eggs (27 ± 9% mean ± SE; n = 22) than in recipient colonies without trophic eggs (83 ± 10%; n = 22; binomial GLMM (link='logit'), z = 4.25, p = 2 × 10–5; Figure 6A and Supplementary file 1, table 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data, statistical analysis, and Figure 6A.

claim: The survival of larvae until the pupal stage was significantly lower in the colonies without trophic eggs (16.9 ± 3.8%) than in colonies with trophic eggs (30.2 ± 6.7%).
source: The survival of larvae until the pupal stage was also significantly lower in the colonies without trophic eggs (16.9 ± 3.8%; n = 22; LMER, z = 2.66, p = 0.008) than in colonies with trophic eggs (30.2 ± 6.7%; mean ± SE; n = 22)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The 1.8-fold survival decrease cannot fully account for the threefold difference in queen percentage between the two treatments.
source: but the 1.8-fold survival decrease cannot fully account for the threefold difference in queen percentage between the two treatments.
evidence: Based on mathematical comparison of the survival and queen percentage differences.

claim: There was no significant correlation between larval mortality and the percentage of larvae developing into queens.
source: Furthermore, there was no significant correlation between larval mortality and the percentage of larvae developing into queens (n = 44 recipient colonies; LMER, z = 0.97, p = 0.34; Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 6B.

claim: Differential survival between castes can be excluded as the sole explanation for the higher percentage of queens developing in the recipient colonies without trophic eggs.
source: These analyses allow us to exclude differential survival between castes as the sole explanation for the higher percentage of queens developing in the recipient colonies without trophic eggs.
evidence: Based on statistical analyses showing no correlation between mortality and queen percentage.

claim: P. rugosus queens lay a very high proportion (0.6) of trophic eggs.
source: Our study reveals that P. rugosus queens lay a very high proportion (0.6) of trophic eggs.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Similar differences between trophic and viable eggs have been reported in other ant species.
source: Similar differences between trophic and viable eggs have been reported in other ant species (Wilson, 1976; Wardlaw and Elmes, 1995; Gobin et al., 1998; Dietemann and Peeters, 2000; Dietemann et al., 2002; Perry and Roitberg, 2006; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Trophic eggs are solely laid by queens in P. rugosus.
source: Our analyses also showed that trophic eggs are solely laid by queens; P. rugosus workers are able to produce viable eggs which occasionally develop into males, but they do not lay trophic eggs.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Trophic eggs have a reduced DNA content compared to viable eggs.
source: Moreover, trophic eggs have a reduced DNA content.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The presence of trophic eggs influences the process of caste determination in P. rugosus.
source: Importantly, our experiments showed that the presence of trophic eggs influences the process of caste determination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the larval caste fate experiment.

claim: First instar female larvae fed with trophic eggs were significantly more likely to develop into workers than larvae without access to trophic eggs.
source: First instar female larvae fed with trophic eggs were significantly more likely to develop into workers than larvae without access to trophic eggs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the larval caste fate experiment.

claim: Trophic eggs are generally thought to be an important source of nutrients to the colony.
source: This was somewhat surprising because trophic eggs are generally thought to be an important source of nutrients to the colony
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding.

claim: One would expect that eating trophic eggs should increase the likelihood of females to develop into queens, everything else being equal.
source: and, everything else being equal, one would think that eating such eggs should increase the likelihood of females to develop into queens (which are usually larger than workers).
evidence: Based on logical inference from the assumption that more nutrients lead to larger body size.

claim: In the two earlier studies on L. humile and P. barbatus, variation in the availability of trophic eggs was associated with other differences, making it difficult to determine what factor had a causal effect.
source: However, in these two studies, variation in the availability of trophic eggs was associated with other differences (number of queens in the colony, Bartels, 1988; Administration of a JH analog, Helms Cahan et al., 2011), making it difficult to determine what factor had a causal effect.
evidence: Based on critical evaluation of cited studies.

claim: A reduced protein content of trophic as compared to viable eggs has been documented in Pheidole pallidula.
source: A reduced protein content of trophic as compared to viable eggs has also been documented in Pheidole pallidula (Lorber and Passera, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The findings that trophic eggs have lower nutrient content are in line with the view that trophic eggs do not simply have a nutritional function.
source: These findings are in line with the view that trophic eggs do not simply have a nutritional function, as it might then be expected that they should at least contain as much nutrients as viable eggs.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the experimental findings.

claim: miRNAs have been suggested to influence larval caste determination in the honeybee.
source: Interestingly, our analyses also revealed important differences in RNA and miRNA content between the two egg types. miRNAs have already been suggested to influence larval caste determination in the honeybee (Guo et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Worker jelly is enriched in miRNAs compared to royal jelly in honeybees.
source: with worker jelly being enriched in miRNAs compared to royal jelly (Guo et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is not the royal jelly that stimulates larval determination into queen in honeybees, but rather the worker jelly which stimulates the development of larvae into workers.
source: These studies suggest that it is not the royal jelly that stimulates larval determination into queen, but rather the worker jelly which stimulates the development of larvae into workers.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Compounds found in trophic eggs, perhaps miRNAs, influence larval development toward the worker phenotype.
source: Similarly, our study reveals that compounds found in trophic eggs, perhaps miRNAs, influence larval development toward the worker phenotype.
evidence: Based on experimental findings and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Trophallactic fluid in the ant Camponotus floridanus contains non-digestive related proteins, microRNAs, and juvenile hormone.
source: Interestingly, it has also been recently shown that trophallactic fluid in the ant Camponotus floridanus contains non-digestive related proteins, microRNAs, and juvenile hormone (LeBoeuf et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Comparison of trophallactic fluid proteins across social insect species revealed that many are regulators of growth, development, and behavioral maturation.
source: Moreover, comparison of trophallactic fluid proteins across social insect species revealed that many are regulators of growth, development, and behavioral maturation (Meurville and LeBoeuf, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Pupae of several ant species produce secretions that play an important role for early larval nutrition.
source: Finally, a recent study showed that pupae of several ant species produce secretions that play an important role for early larval nutrition, with young larvae exhibiting stunted growth and decreased survival without access to the fluid (Snir, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Chemicals delivered in trophic eggs, trophallactic fluids, and pupae secretions may play previously unsuspected roles in communication and caste development.
source: This raises the possibility that chemicals delivered in trophic eggs, trophallactic fluids, and pupae secretions play previously unsuspected roles in communication and caste development.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies and the current findings.

claim: Maternal effects on the process of caste determination have been demonstrated in several social insect species, including P. rugosus.
source: Maternal effects on the process of caste determination have been demonstrated in several social insect species, including P. rugosus, either by queen behavior or content of the eggs being produced (de Menten et al., 2005; Linksvayer, 2006; Schwander et al., 2008; Libbrecht et al., 2013; Wei et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This is the first experimental demonstration that provisioning of trophic eggs influences caste fate.
source: This is, to our knowledge, the first experimental demonstration that provisioning of trophic eggs influences caste fate.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their experimental findings.

claim: Since only queens produce trophic eggs in P. rugosus, trophic egg provisioning could be the main mechanism underlying the previously documented maternal effects on the process of caste determination.
source: Since only queens produce trophic eggs in P. rugosus, trophic egg provisioning could be the main mechanism underlying the previously documented maternal effects on the process of caste determination.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings and previous studies.

claim: In species where workers produce trophic eggs, the same mechanism could allow workers to influence colony level caste ratios if their eggs also affect the process of caste determination.
source: In species where workers produce trophic eggs (Supplementary file 1, table 1), the same mechanism could allow workers to influence colony level caste ratios if their eggs do also affect the process of caste determination.
evidence: Based on speculation extending the findings to other species.

claim: It is likely that trophic eggs are produced in most ant species, particularly in those with an independent mode of colony founding.
source: However, their presence has been investigated in only a few species, and it is likely that trophic eggs are produced in most ant species, particularly in those with an independent mode of colony founding.
evidence: Based on inference from the limited data available and biological reasoning.

claim: There are seasonal differences in the proportion of viable and trophic eggs, with a higher ratio of trophic eggs before hibernation than after.
source: Finally, our analyses also revealed seasonal differences in the proportion of viable and trophic eggs, with a higher ratio of trophic eggs before hibernation than after.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements.

claim: In Pogonomyrmex, the production of new queens occurs after hibernation or when the queen dies or is removed from the colony.
source: In Pogonomyrmex, the production of new queens occurs after hibernation (Smith and Tschinkel, 2006) or when the queen dies or is removed from the colony (pers. obs).
evidence: Supported by citation and personal observations.

claim: New queens are typically produced when there are fewer trophic eggs.
source: Thus, new queens are typically produced when there are fewer trophic eggs.
evidence: Based on inference from the seasonal data and timing of queen production.

claim: Under natural conditions, a decrease in the proportion of trophic eggs should lead to an increase in the proportion of larvae developing into queens.
source: Our results predict that under natural conditions, a decrease in the proportion of trophic eggs should lead to an increase in the proportion of larvae developing into queens.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: After the queen's death, workers start producing their own male offspring and lay mostly (if not only) viable eggs in some species.
source: After the queen's death, workers start producing their own male offspring and lay mostly (if not only) viable eggs (Temnothorax recedens, Dejean and Passera, 1974; Plagiolepis pygmaea, Passera, 1980; Myrmecia gulosa, Dietemann et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A decrease in trophic egg production and the development of queens were observed simultaneously in freshly orphaned colonies of T. recedens, P. pygmaea, and M. gulosa.
source: A decrease in trophic egg production and the development of queens were observed simultaneously in freshly orphaned colonies of T. recedens (Dejean and Passera, 1974), P. pygmaea (Passera, 1980), and M. gulosa (Dietemann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: These examples are consistent with the view that trophic eggs may also play a role in the process of caste determination in other ant species.
source: These examples are consistent with the view that trophic eggs may also play a role in the process of caste determination in other ant species.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Young queens produce more trophic eggs than older queens.
source: In addition to the seasonal differences reported in this study, previous studies in ants have also revealed that young queens produce more trophic eggs than older queens (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The production of new queens in ant colonies starts only when colonies are several years old and have reached a relatively large size.
source: Interestingly, the production of new queens in ant colonies starts only when colonies are several years old and have reached a relatively large size.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ant colony development.

claim: The decrease of the proportion of trophic eggs laid by queens when they age may contribute to the production of new queens being restricted to colonies having reached a relatively large size.
source: Thus, this raises the possibility that the decrease of the proportion of trophic eggs laid by queens when they age may contribute to the production of new queens being restricted to colonies having reached a relatively large size.
evidence: Based on speculation connecting age-related changes in trophic egg production to colony-level patterns.

claim: Egg cannibalism has been reported in many ant species.
source: Egg cannibalism has been reported in many ant species (Wilson, 1971; Sorensen et al., 1983; Bourke, 1991; Crespi, 1977; Peeters and Tsuji, 1993; Aron et al., 1994; Heinze et al., 1999; Schultner et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Egg cannibalism may serve many purposes, including preferential elimination of males, source of energy, and intracolony conflict.
source: and may serve many purposes, including preferential elimination of males, source of energy (Sorensen et al., 1983) and intracolony conflict (Schultner et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Egg cannibalism may serve as a mechanism to regulate the allocation of energy into the production of new queens versus workers.
source: Our study indicates a new potential role of egg cannibalism as a mechanism to regulate the allocation of energy into the production of new queens versus workers.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings about trophic eggs and caste determination.

claim: Some populations of P. rugosus are characterized by a genetic caste determination system whereby development into queens or workers is determined by whether the eggs are fertilized by males of the same genetic lineage or a different genetic lineage than the queen producing the eggs.
source: Some populations of P. rugosus are characterized by a genetic caste determination system whereby development into queens or workers is determined by whether the eggs are fertilized by males of the same genetic lineage or a different genetic lineage than the queen producing the eggs (Cahan et al., 2002; Julian et al., 2002; Volny and Gordon, 2002; Helms Cahan and Keller, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Queens were collected from two populations (Bowie and Florence, Arizona, USA) known to harbor only colonies with non-genetic caste determination.
source: We collected queens from two populations (Bowie and Florence, Arizona, USA) known to harbor only colonies with non-genetic caste determination (Schwander et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study and description of methods.
